title: The Key To Classroom Organization
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin makes the case that a sharp, well-maintained classroom is an overlooked but powerful classroom management tool, since students take their behavioral cues from the physical environment their teacher keeps. He argues that a cluttered room signals that mediocrity is acceptable, regardless of how emphatically a teacher preaches organization. His central organizing principle is 'efficiency': as teachers sort through supplies and materials during a summer overhaul, they should keep only what they truly need to deliver instruction and discard the rest, since 'good teaching is about relationships and preparation and inspiration'—not accumulated stuff. The piece closes by describing the practical and psychological benefits of decluttering, from personal clarity and confidence to the powerful nonverbal message a tidy room sends to students, parents, and administrators.
points: A tidy, well-organized classroom nonverbally communicates an expectation of excellence and personal pride; a cluttered room signals that mediocrity is acceptable.
Teachers must 'walk the walk'—words about neatness ring hollow unless the room itself models the standard.
The guiding principle for a classroom overhaul should be efficiency: keep only what is easiest, quickest, most effective, and truly necessary to deliver curriculum.
'You need far less stuff than you think you do'—good teaching is rooted in relationships, preparation, and inspiration, not accumulated materials.
An organized, efficient classroom yields personal benefits (clarity, confidence, freedom) as well as a powerful nonverbal message to students, parents, and administrators.
quotes: A sharp, well-maintained classroom sends so many wonderful and powerful messages to students—from an expectation of excellence to personal pride in their work habits.

For students take their cue from you, the leader of the classroom. And just as a tidy, clutter-free environment conveys a message of respect and politeness and attention to detail, a messy room signals to all who enter that mediocrity is okay.
So what is this thought, this key to organization? It is efficiency.
The truth is, you need far less ‘stuff’ than you think you do. Good teaching has little to do with the accumulation of materials.
But the real power of organizing your classroom with efficiency as your guide is the impact it will have on your students.
